title: Perfect Squares and Square Roots
seo_title: Grade 7 Perfect Squares and Square Roots Worksheets (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Identify and represent perfect squares, and determine their square roots, in various contexts
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 math worksheets for the Ontario curriculum: perfect squares as square arrays, the squares of 1 to 20, square roots of perfect squares, how to tell if a number is a perfect square, and area and side length word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: A perfect square is a whole number times itself. The square root undoes squaring: 12² = 144, so √144 = 12.
key_sub: 7² means 7 × 7 = 49, not 7 × 2. √36 is 6, not 18: never halve. The side of a square is the square root of its area.
body_html:
What is a perfect square?

A perfect square is a whole number times itself. 5 × 5 = 25, so 25 is a perfect square. We write 5 × 5 as 5² (“5 squared”). The small 2 is an exponent: it tells you to multiply 5 by itself.

A perfect square number of tiles can be set out as a square array, with the same number of rows and columns.

Learn the squares of 1 to 20. They come up again and again.

Example

Evaluate 6² + 8².

6² = 6 × 6 = 36 and 8² = 8 × 8 = 64. Then 36 + 64 = 100.

Answer: 100

Square roots

The square root of a number is the number that, times itself, gives that number. The sign is √. 12 × 12 = 144, so √144 = 12. Squaring and taking the square root undo each other.

For a square, the area is side × side. So the side length is the square root of the area.

Example

What is √1600?

Think: which number times itself is 1600? 40 × 40 = 1600.

Answer: √1600 = 40

Is it a perfect square?

  • Squares on either side. 14² = 196 and 15² = 225, so 200 is not a perfect square.
  • Last digit. A perfect square ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. A number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a perfect square. A good last digit does not prove it, though: 26 ends in 6 and is not a square.
  • Prime factors in pairs. 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = (2 × 3) × (2 × 3) = 6². 18 = 2 × 3 × 3 has a 2 without a partner, so it is not a square.
Example

Is 1000 a perfect square?

31² = 961 and 32² = 1024. 1000 is between them.

Answer: no

Area and side length problems

Example

A square garden has an area of 144 m². How much fencing goes around it?

Side: √144 = 12 m. Perimeter: 4 × 12 = 48 m.

Answer: 48 m of fencing

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead

13² = 19 (squaring each digit)Multiply the whole number: 13 × 13 = 169
√(25 + 144) = √25 + √144Find each root first: 5 + 12 = 17. √169 = 13 is different
Side = area ÷ 4Side = √area. Dividing by 4 works for the perimeter, not the area
“16 is 2 × 8, so it is not a square”Look for any way to make a square: 4 × 4 = 16

faq.q: What is a perfect square in Grade 7 math?
faq.a: A perfect square is a whole number multiplied by itself, such as 49 = 7 × 7 = 7². In the Ontario Grade 7 math curriculum, students show perfect squares as square arrays and find their square roots.

faq.q: How do you find the square root of a perfect square?
faq.a: Ask which whole number times itself gives the number. 12 × 12 = 144, so √144 = 12. Do not divide by 2: √36 is 6, not 18.

faq.q: Which perfect squares should Grade 7 students know?
faq.a: Students should know the squares of 1 to 20, from 1² = 1 to 20² = 400. Knowing them by heart makes square roots, area problems and the Pythagorean theorem in Grade 8 much faster.

faq.q: How do you find the side length of a square from its area?
faq.a: Take the square root of the area. A square garden with an area of 144 m² has sides of √144 = 12 m, so its perimeter is 4 × 12 = 48 m.

items.q: The tiles make a square array. Which perfect square does it show?
items.e: There are 3 rows of 3 tiles: 3 × 3 = 3² = 9. 6 is 3 × 2, 8 counts only the tiles around the edge, and 12 is 3 × 4, a rectangle, not a square.

items.q: The tiles make a square array. Which perfect square does it show?
items.e: There are 5 rows of 5 tiles: 5 × 5 = 5² = 25. 10 is 5 × 2, 16 counts only the tiles around the edge, and 20 is 5 × 4, a rectangle, not a square.

items.q: The tiles make a square array. Which perfect square does it show?
items.e: There are 6 rows of 6 tiles: 6 × 6 = 6² = 36. 12 is 6 × 2, 20 counts only the tiles around the edge, and 42 is 6 × 7, a rectangle, not a square.

items.q: The tiles make a square array. Which perfect square does it show?
items.e: There are 8 rows of 8 tiles: 8 × 8 = 8² = 64. 16 is 8 × 2, 28 counts only the tiles around the edge, and 56 is 8 × 7, a rectangle, not a square.

items.q: Which array is a square array?
items.e: A square array has the same number of rows and columns. B has 4 rows of 4 tiles, so B is a square and shows 4² = 16. A is 3 × 4 = 12, C is 3 × 6 = 18 and D is 2 × 8 = 16 tiles in a rectangle.

items.q: Which array shows a perfect square?
items.e: D has 5 rows of 5 tiles: 5² = 25, so D shows a perfect square. A, B and C each have 24 tiles (4 × 6, 3 × 8, 2 × 12). 24 tiles cannot make a square, because no whole number times itself is 24.

items.q: These 30 tiles make 5 rows of 6. How many more tiles are needed to make a 6 × 6 square array?
items.e: 6 × 6 = 36 and 36 − 30 = 6. That is one more row of 6 tiles. A row of 5 is too short, and 11 adds a row and a column.

items.q: The green tiles make a 6 × 6 square. How many orange tiles turn it into the next square, 7 × 7?
items.e: 7² − 6² = 49 − 36 = 13. The new row has 7 tiles and the new column has 6 more (the corner is counted once). 12 forgets the corner tile and 14 counts it twice.

items.q: A square array has 81 tiles. How many tiles are in each row?
items.e: In a square array, rows × rows = 81. 9 × 9 = 81, so there are 9 tiles in each row. 40.5 is 81 ÷ 2, 20.25 is 81 ÷ 4 and 27 is 81 ÷ 3.

items.q: Which number of tiles can be set out as a square array?
items.e: 8 × 8 = 64, so 64 tiles make a square array. 24, 32 and 48 are multiples of 8, but none of them is a whole number times itself.

items.q: Which number of tiles cannot be set out as a square array?
The pattern grows by one row and one column each time. How many tiles are in the next array?
items.e: The next array is 4 × 4 = 16. The squares go up by 3, 5, 7 …: 9 + 7 = 16. 14 adds 5 again and 12 adds 3 again.

items.q: The perfect squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 go up by 3, 5, 7, 9 … What is the perfect square after 100?
items.e: 100 = 10² and the next square is 11² = 121. It is 100 + 21, because 10 + 11 = 21. 119 adds 19 again (81 to 100 added 19), 110 adds 10 and 102 adds 2.

items.q: Which statement describes this array?
items.e: There are 7 rows of 7 tiles, so the array shows 7² = 49. 7² means 7 × 7, not 7 × 2 or 7 + 7. 4 × 7 = 28 adds the four sides and counts each corner twice.

items.q: Amira has 40 tiles. What is the largest square array she can make?
items.e: 6 × 6 = 36 uses 36 tiles (4 are left over). 7 × 7 = 49 needs 9 more tiles than Amira has. So the largest is 6 by 6. 20 by 20 comes from halving 40.

items.q: A square array has 12 tiles in each row. How many tiles are there altogether?
items.e: 12 rows of 12: 12² = 12 × 12 = 144. 24 is 12 × 2, 48 is 4 × 12 (the four sides), and 132 is 12 × 11, one row short.

items.q: Sofia sets out 16 tiles as 2 rows of 8. She says this shows 16 is not a perfect square. Is she right?
c: No. 16 tiles also make 4 rows of 4
Yes. 2 rows of 8 is not a square
items.e: A number is a perfect square if its tiles can make a square. 4 × 4 = 16, so 16 is a perfect square, even though 2 × 8 is a rectangle.

items.q: A square array has 11 rows of 11 tiles. Which perfect square does it show?
items.e: 11 × 11 = 11² = 121. 22 is 11 × 2, 111 just writes another 1, and 40 counts only the tiles around the edge (4 × 11 − 4).

items.q: How many more tiles does a 9 × 9 array have than an 8 × 8 array?
items.e: 9² − 8² = 81 − 64 = 17. The difference is not 1: the bigger square has a whole extra row and column. 16 is 8 + 8 and 18 is 9 + 9; the right answer is 8 + 9 = 17.

items.q: A square array has 10 000 tiles. How many tiles are in each row?
items.e: 100 × 100 = 10 000, so there are 100 tiles in each row. 5000 is half of 10 000, 2500 is a quarter, and 1000 × 1000 = 1 000 000.

items.q: What is 7²?
What is 9²?
What is 11²?
items.e: 11² means 11 × 11 = 121. 22 is 11 × 2, 111 just adds another 1, and 110 is 11 × 10.

items.q: What is 12²?
items.e: 12² means 12 × 12 = 144. 24 is 12 × 2, 132 is 12 × 11, and 14 squares each digit (1² = 1, 2² = 4).

items.q: What is 13²?
items.e: 13² means 13 × 13 = 169. 26 is 13 × 2, 19 squares each digit (1² = 1, 3² = 9), and 156 is 13 × 12.

items.q: What is 15²?
items.e: 15² means 15 × 15 = 225. 30 is 15 × 2, 125 squares each digit (1² = 1, 5² = 25), and 210 is 15 × 14.

items.q: What is 16²?
items.e: 16² means 16 × 16 = 256. 32 is 16 × 2, 136 squares each digit (1² = 1, 6² = 36), and 240 is 16 × 15.

items.q: What is 18²?
items.e: 18² means 18 × 18 = 324. 36 is 18 × 2, 164 squares each digit (1² = 1, 8² = 64), and 306 is 18 × 17.

items.q: What is 19²?
items.e: 19² means 19 × 19 = 361. 38 is 19 × 2, 181 squares each digit (1² = 1, 9² = 81), and 342 is 19 × 18.

items.q: What is 20²?
items.e: 20² means 20 × 20 = 400. 40 is 20 × 2, 200 is 20 × 10, and 4000 has one zero too many.

items.q: Zoe writes 7² = 14. What mistake did she make?
items.e: The small 2 is an exponent. It means “multiply 7 by itself”: 7² = 7 × 7 = 49, not 7 × 2 = 14.

items.q: Which whole number squared is 196?
Which square is closest to 300?
items.e: 17² = 289 is 11 away from 300, and 18² = 324 is 24 away. So 17² is closest. 15² = 225 is too small, and 150 is half of 300.

items.q: Which list shows 11², 12², 13², 14² and 15²?
Evaluate 6² + 8².
items.e: 6² = 36 and 8² = 64. 36 + 64 = 100. 28 comes from 6 × 2 + 8 × 2, 196 from adding first (14²), and 48 from 6 × 8.

items.q: Evaluate 13² − 12².
items.e: 13² = 169 and 12² = 144. 169 − 144 = 25. 1 comes from subtracting first (1²), 2 from 26 − 24, and 313 from adding instead of subtracting.

items.q: Evaluate (−5)².
items.e: (−5)² = (−5) × (−5). A negative times a negative is positive, so the answer is 25. −10 and 10 come from multiplying by 2, and −25 forgets that the two negatives make a positive.

items.q: Evaluate 2 × 5².
items.e: Exponents come before multiplication: 5² = 25, then 2 × 25 = 50. 100 squares 2 × 5 = 10 first, 20 is 2 × 5 × 2, and 25 forgets the 2 ×.

items.q: Jayden says 30² = 90. What is 30²?
items.e: 30² = 30 × 30 = 3 × 3 × 10 × 10 = 900. 90 squares the 3 but keeps only one zero, 60 is 30 × 2, and 9000 has one zero too many.

items.q: How many perfect squares are there between 100 and 200?
items.e: 11² = 121, 12² = 144, 13² = 169 and 14² = 196. That is 4. 15² = 225 is too big, and 100 is not between 100 and 200. Do not forget 196.

items.q: What is √36?
What is √49?
What is √64?
What is √81?
What is √121?
What is √144?
What is √169?
What is √225?
items.e: 15 × 15 = 225, so √225 = 15. 112.5 is 225 ÷ 2, 25 only looks at the last two digits, and 5 is √25.

items.q: What is √256?
What is √400?
items.e: 20 × 20 = 400, so √400 = 20. A perfect square ending in two zeros has a root ending in one zero. 200 is 400 ÷ 2, 40 × 40 = 1600, and 2 is √4 with the zeros dropped.

items.q: What is √900?
items.e: 30 × 30 = 900, so √900 = 30. A perfect square ending in two zeros has a root ending in one zero. 450 is 900 ÷ 2, 300 × 300 = 90 000, and 3 is √9 with the zeros dropped.

items.q: What is √1600?
items.e: 40 × 40 = 1600, so √1600 = 40. A perfect square ending in two zeros has a root ending in one zero. 800 is 1600 ÷ 2, 400 × 400 = 160 000, and 4 is √16 with the zeros dropped.

items.q: What is √10 000?
Which square root equals 9?
Owen says √36 = 18. What mistake did he make?
items.e: The square root is the number that, times itself, gives 36. 6 × 6 = 36, so √36 = 6. 18 × 18 = 324, not 36. Dividing by 2 is not the same as taking the square root.

items.q: Evaluate √25 + √144.
items.e: √25 = 5 and √144 = 12, so 5 + 12 = 17. 13 comes from adding first: √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13. That is not allowed: find each root first. 169 forgets the roots, and 84.5 halves 169.

items.q: Evaluate √64 − √16.
items.e: √64 = 8 and √16 = 4, so 8 − 4 = 4. 48 is 64 − 16 with no roots, 24 is 32 − 8 (halving), and 12 adds the roots instead of subtracting.

items.q: √x = 14. What is x?
Evaluate √(4 × 25).
items.e: 4 × 25 = 100 and √100 = 10. You can also find √4 × √25 = 2 × 5 = 10. 50 halves 100, 100 forgets the root, and 7 adds 2 + 5.

items.q: Which square root is a whole number?
items.e: 64 is a perfect square (8 × 8), so √64 = 8. 32, 12 and 50 are not perfect squares, so their square roots are not whole numbers. √32 is not 16: 16 × 16 = 256.

items.q: Which number is a perfect square?
items.e: 8 × 8 = 64, so 64 is a perfect square. 32 = 4 × 8, 24 = 4 × 6 and 48 = 6 × 8: none is a whole number times itself.

items.q: Which number is a perfect square?
items.e: 11 × 11 = 121. 10² = 100 and 11² = 121, so 111 and 112 fall between two squares. 22 is 11 × 2.

items.q: Which number is not a perfect square?
items.e: 36 = 6², 100 = 10² and 144 = 12². 9² = 81 and 10² = 100, so 90 is not a perfect square. Ending in 0 like 100 is not enough.

items.q: Which number is not a perfect square?
items.e: 25 = 5², 225 = 15² and 625 = 25². 11² = 121 and 12² = 144, so 125 is not a perfect square. (125 = 5 × 5 × 5.) Ending in 25 is not enough.

items.q: Is 196 a perfect square?
items.e: 14 × 14 = 196, so yes, 196 = 14². Being even does not matter (4, 16 and 36 are even squares). 98 × 2 is a product of two different numbers, so it does not show a square.

items.q: Is 200 a perfect square?
items.e: 200 lies between 14² = 196 and 15² = 225, so no whole number squared makes 200. 100 × 2 and 20 × 10 are not a number times itself.

items.q: Is 1000 a perfect square?
items.e: 1000 lies between 31² = 961 and 32² = 1024, so it is not a perfect square. 10 × 10 × 10 = 10³ uses three factors, not two equal factors.

items.q: A perfect square can never end in which digit?
items.e: The squares of 0 to 9 end in 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1. So a perfect square can end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. It can never end in 2, 3, 7 or 8. 81 ends in 1, 16 in 6 and 49 in 9.

items.q: Which number cannot be a perfect square? Look at the last digit.
items.e: No perfect square ends in 8, so 2028 cannot be one. The others are squares: 45² = 2025, 44² = 1936 and 46² = 2116.

items.q: How many perfect squares are there between 50 and 100?
items.e: 8² = 64 and 9² = 81. That is 2. 7² = 49 is below 50, and 100 is not between 50 and 100.

items.q: Which list has only perfect squares?
items.e: 1 = 1², 4 = 2², 9 = 3² and 16 = 4², so 1, 4, 9, 16 are all perfect squares. 2, 6, 8 and 24 are not.

items.q: Which product is a perfect square?
items.e: In a perfect square, the prime factors come in pairs. 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = (2 × 3) × (2 × 3) = 6 × 6 = 36, so 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 is a perfect square. 2 × 3 × 3 = 18, 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24 and 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 each have a prime without a partner.

items.q: Which number has an odd number of factors?
items.e: Factors come in pairs, but in a perfect square one pair is a number times itself (6 × 6), so it is counted once. 36 has 9 factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. So the answer is 36. 24, 30 and 40 each have 8 factors.

items.q: Mei says 50 is a perfect square because 25 × 2 = 50. Is she right?
c: No. No whole number times itself is 50
items.e: A perfect square is a whole number times itself. 7² = 49 and 8² = 64, so 50 is not a perfect square. 25 × 2 uses two different numbers. Being even is not the reason: 64 is even and square.

items.q: What is the smallest perfect square greater than 150?
items.e: 12² = 144 is less than 150. The next square is 13² = 169. 160 is not a square, and 196 = 14² is the square after 169.

items.q: What is the largest perfect square less than 300?
items.e: 17² = 289 and 18² = 324. 324 is more than 300, so the answer is 289. 256 = 16² is smaller than 289, and 299 is not a square.

items.q: Which number is a perfect square and odd?
items.e: 81 = 9², and 81 is odd, so the answer is 81. 64 = 8² is even, and 99 and 27 are odd but not perfect squares (27 = 3 × 3 × 3).

items.q: By which number can you multiply 18 to get a perfect square?
items.e: 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. The 2 has no partner, so multiply by 2: 18 × 2 = 36 = 6². 18 × 3 = 54, 18 × 4 = 72 and 18 × 9 = 162 are not perfect squares.

items.q: Which number is a perfect square?
items.e: 50 × 50 = 2500. A whole number ending in zeros can be a square only if it ends in an even number of zeros (100, 2500, 10 000). 250 and 25 000 end in an odd number of zeros, and 5000 is double 2500.

items.q: Maya says every number ending in 6 is a perfect square, like 16 and 36. Which number shows she is wrong?
items.e: 5² = 25 and 6² = 36, so 26 is not a perfect square, even though it ends in 6. 16 = 4², 36 = 6² and 196 = 14². The last digit can rule a number out, but it cannot prove it is a square.

sets.title: Word problems: area and side length

items.q: A square garden has an area of 144 m². How long is each side?
items.e: The area of a square is side × side. 12 × 12 = 144, so each side is √144 = 12 m. 72 m halves the area, 36 m divides the area by 4, mixing it up with perimeter, and 24 m is 12 × 2.

items.q: A square garden has an area of 144 m². How many metres of fence go all the way around it?
items.e: First find the side: √144 = 12 m. The fence goes around 4 sides: 4 × 12 = 48 m. 12 m is only one side, and 576 m is 4 × 144, using the area instead of the side.

items.q: A square floor tile is 30 cm on each side. What is its area?
items.e: Area = side × side = 30 × 30 = 900 cm². 60 is 30 × 2, 120 cm is the perimeter (4 × 30), and 90 forgets one zero.

items.q: Kai’s family floods a square backyard rink with an area of 81 m². How long is each side?
items.e: 9 × 9 = 81, so each side is √81 = 9 m. 40.5 halves 81, 20.25 divides it by 4, and 27 divides it by 3.

items.q: Mateo sews a square quilt from 64 square patches. How many patches are in each row?
items.e: The quilt is a square array, so rows × rows = 64. 8 × 8 = 64, so there are 8 patches in each row. 32 is 64 ÷ 2, 16 is 64 ÷ 4, and 4 × 4 = 16, not 64.

items.q: A square photo has an area of 225 cm². How long is each side?
items.e: 15 × 15 = 225, so each side is √225 = 15 cm. 112.5 halves 225, 56.25 divides it by 4, and 25 only looks at the last two digits (25 × 25 = 625).

items.q: The 121 students in a school band march in a square formation. How many students are in each row?
items.e: 11 × 11 = 121, so there are 11 students in each row. 60.5 and 30.25 are not whole students, and 12 × 12 = 144.

items.q: 150 students stand in the largest square formation they can for a Terry Fox Run photo. How many students are left out of the square?
items.e: 12² = 144 and 13² = 169. 169 is too many, so the square is 12 by 12 = 144 students. 150 − 144 = 6 are left out. 19 is how many more students a 13 by 13 square would need.

items.q: A square vegetable patch is 6 m on each side. The side length is doubled to 12 m. What is the new area?
items.e: 12 × 12 = 144 m². The old area was 6 × 6 = 36 m², so doubling the side makes the area 4 times as big, not 2 times (72 m²). 48 m is the new perimeter.

items.q: A square sandbox has a perimeter of 24 m. What is its area?
items.e: Each side is 24 ÷ 4 = 6 m. The area is 6 × 6 = 36 m². 144 comes from 12 × 12 (24 ÷ 2), 576 is 24 × 24, and the area is not the same as the perimeter.

items.q: A square bulletin board has an area of 1.44 m². How long is each side?
Emma paints on a square canvas that is 50 cm on each side. What is the area of the canvas?
items.e: 50 × 50 = 2500 cm². 100 is 50 × 2, 200 cm is the perimeter (4 × 50), and 250 has one zero too few.

items.q: A square soccer practice field has an area of 900 m². Ava runs once around its edge. How far does she run?
items.e: Each side is √900 = 30 m. Once around is 4 × 30 = 120 m. 30 m is only one side, 225 is 900 ÷ 4 (dividing the area, not the perimeter), and 3600 is 4 × 900.

items.q: A square garden with an area of 196 m² is split into 4 equal square beds, 2 rows of 2. How long is each side of one bed?
items.e: The garden is √196 = 14 m on each side. Two beds fit across, so each bed is 14 ÷ 2 = 7 m on each side. Check: 7 × 7 = 49 m², and 4 × 49 = 196. 49 is the area of a bed, not its side.

items.q: Two square gardens have areas of 64 m² and 100 m². How much longer is a side of the larger garden?
items.e: The sides are √64 = 8 m and √100 = 10 m. 10 − 8 = 2 m. 6 m comes from √(100 − 64) = √36: find each root first. 36 is the difference in area, and 18 is 8 + 10.

items.q: Ethan makes a square mosaic with 15 small tiles along each side. How many tiles does he use?
items.e: 15 rows of 15: 15² = 225 tiles. 30 is 15 × 2, 60 is the 4 sides (4 × 15), and 56 counts only the tiles around the edge (4 × 15 − 4).

items.q: A square outdoor rink has an area of 256 m². How many metres of boards go all the way around it?
items.e: Each side is √256 = 16 m (16 × 16 = 256). The boards go around 4 sides: 4 × 16 = 64 m. 16 m is one side, 128 halves the area, and 1024 is 4 × 256.

items.q: A square school garden has an area of 400 m². A row of sunflowers will be planted along one side. How long is the row?
items.e: One side is √400 = 20 m (20 × 20 = 400). 200 halves the area, 100 is 400 ÷ 4, and 80 m is the whole perimeter (4 × 20).

items.q: A square deck is 8 m on each side. It is made bigger so each side is 10 m. How many square metres of decking are added?
items.e: New area: 10² = 100 m². Old area: 8² = 64 m². 100 − 64 = 36 m². 2 m is only the change in side length, 4 m² is 2², and 16 m² adds one strip of 2 × 8.

items.q: Noah’s cottage has a square dock with an area of 169 m². He walks once around the edge. How far does he walk?
items.e: Each side is √169 = 13 m. Once around is 4 × 13 = 52 m. 13 m is only one side, 42.25 is 169 ÷ 4, and 676 is 4 × 169.
